summary:
Enugu State lies wholly within Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches conduct well beyond marriage: cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. The law also reaches those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding, according to the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026. Human Rights Watch recorded in October 2016 that police have invoked the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. Trans identity is not expressly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed through that enforcement culture.

The same FCDO advice warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. It states that same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and that some northern states apply Sharia provisions capable of prescribing the death penalty. The advice therefore places a visitor to Enugu under national exposure at the border and in any onward travel to the north.

Violence against perceived LGBT people is a routine feature of the environment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation documented in April 2024 kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar applications to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a risk that applies to dating-app use in Enugu as elsewhere. Police extortion on the basis of perceived sexuality is documented as well: in March 2025 TimesLIVE reported that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing with little accountability. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial reported in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Healthcare access inside Enugu State is constrained by the same hostility. An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community, and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, forcing many to travel to Lagos and other states. A visitor needing sexual-health or trans-related care should therefore expect to leave the state to find services that can be used without exposure.

Detention carries an unresolved placement risk for trans visitors. Press coverage of the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion rather than to a rule.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced criminalisation inherited from the colonial era. Enugu State has no separate statutory layer of its own in the sources available, so the state-level position is the national position.

Legislative turbulence is unresolved. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here, and a visitor cannot assume the current text of the law from that reporting alone.

The closest state-level documentation of Enugu's position is Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report, which is a decade old. Enforcement patterns since then are evidenced only through national reporting from Lagos, Abuja and other cities, which is how the pattern described above was established rather than from Enugu-specific arrests.

The care deficit described for Enugu has a geographic consequence: services are sought in Lagos and other states, which exposes a visitor to repeated travel between jurisdictions under a law that applies identically throughout the country.
localsOnly:
Residents of Enugu State live under the full reach of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which criminalises cohabitation between same-sex partners, public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and which extends to those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding. Human Rights Watch documented police use of the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Social and family pressure pushes people into formal heterosexual arrangements. Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told Human Rights Watch that she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, adding, 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.'

An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community, and that no clinics exist where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, so many travel to Lagos and other states for care.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Not sourced: whether Enugu State has its own anti-discrimination, hate-crime or public-order provisions directed at gender expression, independent of the national statute. No state-level instrument appears in the inventory.

Not sourced: any Enugu-specific arrest, prosecution or police-violence statistics. The only state-level evidence in the inventory is Human Rights Watch's October 2016 account of care access and one resident's marriage under social pressure.

Not sourced: entry, visa or immigration screening practice for trans travellers arriving in Nigeria, including whether passport gender markers are examined or challenged on arrival.

Unresolved: whether a general rule governs the placement of trans detainees in Nigerian prisons. The Bobrisky case shows discretion at sentencing and a later finding on the conditions of her housing, but no sourced standard applying to other detainees.

Not sourced: whether the health-service gap described for Enugu State in 2016 has since narrowed, or the current availability of clinics serving men who have sex with men without harassment.
